summary: A team may replace players only while play is stopped, with the referee's permission. The player coming off leaves promptly at the nearest point, the replacement waits at the halfway line until the referee signals, and the change is complete once the replacement steps onto the field. How many changes a team gets depends on the competition.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 3: The Players

summary: A player sent off after the match has started cannot be replaced, so the team plays on with one fewer player. A team that is reduced below seven players cannot continue the match.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 3: The Players
keywords: sent off dismissed ejected straight red sent off red card replace replacement down a player

summary: When a foul happens, the referee may let play continue if the fouled team stands to gain. If the expected benefit does not appear within a few seconds, the referee comes back and punishes the original offence; any card is usually shown when play next stops.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 5: The Referee
plain: Advantage means the referee lets play carry on after a foul because the fouled team is still in a good position, instead of stopping the game.

summary: Video review may only help the referee correct a clear and obvious mistake or a serious missed incident involving goals, penalties, direct red cards or mistaken identity. source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 5: The Referee
plain: VAR is a team of video referees who watch the game on screens. They step in only for clear mistakes about goals, penalties, direct red cards or the wrong player being punished, and the referee on the field still makes the final decision.

summary: A match has two equal halves of 45 minutes with a break of up to 15 minutes. At the end of each half the referee adds time for stoppages such as substitutions, injuries, time-wasting, discipline, drinks breaks, video reviews and goal celebrations, and a half is extended to finish a penalty kick.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 7: The Duration of the Match
keywords: added time injury time stoppage time why extra minutes

law_title: The Start and Restart of Play
summary: Play starts, and restarts after a goal, with a kick-off from the centre mark. The ball must be still and every player except the kicker must be in their own half. The ball is in play once it is kicked and clearly moves, and a goal may be scored directly from it against the opponents.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 8: The Start and Restart of Play

law_title: The Start and Restart of Play
summary: If the referee stops play when no free kick or other restart applies, the ball is dropped for one player of the team that was in control, or for the defending goalkeeper inside the penalty area. A goal cannot count from a dropped ball unless at least two players have touched it.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 8: The Start and Restart of Play

law_title: The Ball In and Out of Play
summary: The ball is out of play once all of it has crossed the goal line or touchline, or when the referee stops play. It remains in play if it bounces back off a goalpost, crossbar or corner flag and stays on the field.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 9: The Ball In and Out of Play

law_title: Determining the Outcome of a Match
summary: A goal counts when the whole ball passes over the goal line between the posts and under the crossbar, as long as the scoring team has not committed an offence. The team with more goals wins; equal goals is a draw unless the competition requires a winner.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 10: Determining the Outcome of a Match

law_title: Determining the Outcome of a Match
summary: Where a winner is needed, competitions may use extra time and a shoot-out of alternating penalty kicks. Each team takes five kicks, then single kicks until one side leads after an equal number, and only players on the field at the final whistle may take part.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 10: Determining the Outcome of a Match

summary: A player is considered in an offside position only in the opponents' half and when nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent. A position alone is not an offence; the player must then become involved in active play.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 11: Offside
keywords: offside flag linesman assistant second last defender
plain: Offside is a rule that stops attackers from just waiting next to the other team's goal. When a teammate passes the ball forward, an attacker must not be closer to the goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender (the goalkeeper usually counts as one of the defenders). Standing there is not a foul by itself: the referee only gives offside if that player then joins in, for example by playing the ball or getting in a defender's way. The other team then gets a free kick.

summary: An attacker in an offside position is only penalised if they take part in play when a team-mate passes the ball. That means playing the ball, getting in an opponent's way or clearly affecting their ability to play it, or benefiting from a ball that rebounds off a post, an opponent or a deliberate save. The position is judged at the moment of the pass, and the restart is an indirect free kick.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 11: Offside
keywords: offside flag linesman assistant second last defender

summary: Body parts that can score count when judging offside, but arms and hands do not. A player level with the second-last opponent is not offside, and there is no offside offence when the ball comes directly from a goal kick, a throw-in or a corner kick.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 11: Offside
keywords: offside flag linesman assistant second last defender

summary: A tackle, charge, trip, push or similar challenge is a foul if the referee judges it careless, reckless or made with excessive force. Careless earns a free kick, reckless earns a free kick and a caution, and excessive force earns a free kick and a sending-off; a foul inside the defender's own penalty area gives a penalty kick.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct

summary: A foul that stops or interferes with a promising attack can be punished as unsporting behaviour with a caution. The referee considers the attack's direction, distance from goal, likelihood of control and the positions of other players.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct

summary: A yellow card caution is shown for offences such as unsporting behaviour, reckless challenges, dissent, delaying a restart, persistent fouling and stopping a promising attack. A caution marks a warning for the player and does not by itself remove them from the match.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct
plain: A yellow card is a warning to a player. It is shown for things like a reckless tackle, wasting time, arguing with the referee or a foul that stops a promising attack. It does not send the player off.

summary: A red card sends a player off for offences such as serious foul play, violent conduct, spitting or biting, abusive language, denying an obvious goal-scoring opportunity, or a second caution in the same match. The player must leave the field and cannot be replaced.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct
keywords: sent off dismissed ejected straight red
plain: A red card sends a player off for the rest of the match, and their team has to play one player short because they cannot be replaced. It is shown for very serious things, such as dangerous or violent play, fouling to stop an obvious goal chance, or a second yellow card in the same match.

summary: A defender who commits a foul that denies an opponent an obvious chance to score is normally sent off. The referee weighs the distance to goal, the direction of play, the chance of keeping or winning the ball and where the defenders are. If a penalty is given and the defender was genuinely trying to play the ball, a caution is enough.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct
keywords: sent off dismissed ejected straight red

summary: Serious foul play is a challenge for the ball that endangers an opponent's safety or uses excessive force or brutality, for example lunging in with a leg. It is punished by a sending-off and a direct free kick, or a penalty kick if it happens in the offender's penalty area.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct
keywords: sent off dismissed ejected straight red

summary: A player who receives a second caution in the same match is shown a yellow card and then a red card and must leave the field. The team continues a player short.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct

summary: Handball is a free-kick offence when a player deliberately touches the ball with the hand or arm, or makes the body unnaturally larger so the arm blocks or touches it. Scoring with the hand or arm is an offence even if accidental. The arm's upper limit is the bottom of the armpit.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 12: Fouls and Misconduct
plain: Handball means deliberately touching the ball with the hand or arm, or making your body unnaturally bigger so your arm blocks the ball. It gives the other team a free kick, or a penalty if it happens in the defender's own box.

summary: A free kick is taken from where the offence happened, with the ball still, and the kicker may not touch it again until another player has. A direct free kick may score straight into the opponents' goal, an indirect kick must touch another player first, and opponents must stand at least 9.15 metres away.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 13: Free Kicks
plain: A free kick restarts play after a foul. The ball is placed where the foul happened and the other team must stay about nine metres away. A direct free kick can go straight into the goal, while an indirect one must touch another player first.

summary: A penalty kick is awarded for a direct-free-kick offence committed by a defender inside that team's penalty area while the ball is in play. The ball is placed on the penalty mark, the kicker is identified and the other players take the positions required by the procedure.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 14: The Penalty Kick
keywords: penalty spot spot kick area foul
plain: A penalty is a free shot at goal from 11 metres, given when a defender commits a foul inside their own penalty box. Only the kicker and the goalkeeper take part, and everyone else waits outside the box.

summary: At a penalty kick the goalkeeper must stay on the goal line until the ball is kicked. If the ball is saved, misses the goal or rebounds off the frame without any offence, play simply continues from that point, and a goal is scored only if the ball ends up in the net. A kick is retaken if the defence breaks the procedure and the kick is saved or missed.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 14: The Penalty Kick

summary: A throw-in goes to the opponents of the team that last touched the ball when all of it crossed the touchline. The thrower faces the field, keeps part of each foot on or behind the line and throws with both hands from behind and over the head. A goal cannot be scored directly from it, and there is no offside offence from a throw-in.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 15: The Throw-in

summary: A goal kick is awarded to the defending team when the whole ball crosses their goal line after last touching an attacker and no goal is scored. It is kicked from inside the goal area and is in play once it is kicked and clearly moves.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 16: The Goal Kick
keywords: goal kick goal kick defender restart

summary: A corner kick goes to the attacking team when the whole ball crosses the goal line after last touching a defender, without a goal. It is taken from the corner arc nearest to where the ball left the field, with opponents at least 9.15 metres away, and a goal may be scored directly from it against the opponents.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 17: The Corner Kick
plain: A corner kick goes to the attacking team when the ball crosses the goal line after a defender touched it last. The ball is placed in the corner and kicked into play, and the other team must stay about nine metres away.

summary: The pitch may be natural grass, or artificial or hybrid turf where the competition rules permit it, and any artificial surface must be green.

keywords: lines touchline goal line halfway centre circle spot

source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 1: The Field of Play

summary: The touchlines must be longer than the goal lines. In general the pitch is 90 to 120 metres long and 45 to 90 metres wide, while international matches use 100 to 110 metres by 64 to 75 metres.

summary: The goal area is the small box in front of each goal, reaching 5.5 metres out from each post and 5.5 metres into the field. Goal kicks are taken from inside it.

keywords: eighteen yard box penalty area penalty mark arc d
summary: The penalty area extends 16.5 metres from each post and 16.5 metres into the field, with the penalty mark 11 metres from the goal. An arc of 9.15 metre radius is drawn outside the box from the penalty mark. A defender's foul inside this area is punished by a penalty kick.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 1: The Field of Play

summary: Each corner has a flagpost and a quarter circle of one metre radius, which is where the ball is placed for a corner kick.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 1: The Field of Play

keywords: goalposts crossbar net width height how big size dimensions goal width height

source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 1: The Field of Play

keywords: goal line technology gl sensor ball crossed line

source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 1: The Field of Play

keywords: video operation room referee review area monitor
summary: Video-assisted matches have a video operation room and a marked referee review area beside the field. Entering the video room is a sending-off offence, and entering the review area is a caution.

summary: The ball must be round, made of suitable material, about 68 to 70 cm around and 410 to 450 grams at the start. Official competitions allow only the competition, organiser and manufacturer marks on it.

summary: If the ball bursts or becomes defective, play stops and restarts with a dropped ball, unless it happened at a restart, in which case that restart is retaken. The ball can only be changed with the referee's permission.

keywords: seven players minimum eleven team size abandon how many players number of players team size
summary: A team has at most eleven players including its goalkeeper, and a match cannot begin or carry on if either team has fewer than seven. Players sent off count against the team, so a team down to six ends the match.

summary: Any outfield player can take over as goalkeeper, provided the referee is told first and the change happens while play is stopped.

keywords: extra person coach substitute interfere outside agent
summary: If someone not allowed on the field, such as a substitute or official, interferes with play, the referee stops play, removes them and takes disciplinary action. Interference by an outside agent leads to a dropped ball.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 3: The Players

summary: Players may not wear anything dangerous, and all jewellery is banned. Equipment is checked before kick-off, and substitutes are checked before they come on.

keywords: shirt shorts socks shinguards boots captain armband

summary: The two teams must wear colours that clearly differ from each other and from the match officials, and goalkeepers must differ from everyone else on the field.

summary: Light protective items such as gloves, headgear and padding are allowed. Players and substitutes may not use electronic communication devices, apart from approved performance-tracking equipment.
source_title: IFAB Laws of the Game — Law 4: The Players' Equipment

summary: Shirts and undergarments must not carry political, religious or personal slogans or offensive images. Names, numbers, crests and approved sponsors are normally fine.

keywords: incorrect equipment leave field fix re-enter

summary: The referee has full authority to apply the Laws, acts as timekeeper, keeps the match record and reports misconduct. Injured players generally have to leave the field for treatment, and a bleeding player must stay off until the bleeding has stopped.

summary: The referee's decisions on facts of play, including whether a goal was scored and the result, are final. A restart decision cannot be changed once play has restarted.

keywords: two offences same time more serious
